item.title: Firefighting Helicopter Crashes Near Utah Wildfire, Killing Two Onboard
item.description:
A helicopter battling one of the nation’s largest active wildfires crashed while navigating treacherous terrain in central Utah on Friday, killing the two firefighters who were on board, according to federal officials.

The aircraft, one of several fighting the fast-spreading Widemouth 2 blaze burning through Fishlake National Forest and the surrounding communities, went down near the city of Richfield around 10 a.m. The wreck sparked another fire, officials said, and flames quickly overran the area, initially preventing emergency personnel from reaching the site.

“No escape routes that any firefighters could get into or out of if we had put them in there,” said Nathan Curtis, the sheriff of Sevier County, where the crash occurred.

Overnight, the authorities remained uncertain about the fate of the pilot and crew member aboard the helicopter, which had been working on contract with the U.S. Forest Service, but by Saturday morning their worst fears had been confirmed.

The National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of federal and state agencies, reported their deaths in its daily bulletin.

Officials have not identified the firefighters, and they were still working to determine the cause of the crash. Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board traveled to the area but were waiting for fire conditions to improve before they could reach the crash site, said a spokeswoman for the agency, Sarah Taylor Sulick.

In an unsigned statement, the Forest Service said only that it was “an emerging situation” and that “safety actions are prioritized first.”

But even as many central questions remained unanswered, Friday’s fatalities deepened an already solemn mood that has taken hold at base camps and incident command centers across the West this year, as a raging wildfire season has claimed the lives of several other first responders. In June, three wildland firefighters died while battling a blaze along the Utah-Colorado border, and on Thursday a bulldozer operator was killed in a southern Oregon fire.

“Wildland firefighting is among the most dangerous jobs in the world,” Gov. Spencer Cox of Utah said in a statement on Friday, responding to the crash in his state. “Today is a painful reminder of the extraordinary risks these brave men and women accept to protect us.”

Authorities believe the Widemouth 2 fire began with a lightning strike on July 27 and quickly scorched more than 100,000 acres, feasting on tinder-dry forests and propelled by unpredictable winds. It is the latest large blaze in what researchers say is one of the state’s worst fire seasons on record, with Utah — and the rest of the West — struggling through a brutal drought and sweltering summer.

“This is our third fire to be right at 100,000 acres this year, which is not a record that we’re proud of,” Mr. Cox told reporters during a tour of the fire line on Thursday. He said the fierce fire season had exhausted emergency workers and spread resources thin.

When the firefighting helicopter, a Sikorsky S64, took off on Friday morning, conditions were safe enough to fly, Tyler Hecht, a deputy commander with the Great Basin Incident Management Team, said at a news briefing later that day. The terrain was steep and tricky, Mr. Hecht said, but it was not unusual for this type of wildfire.

As Widemouth 2 continued to rage, with just about a quarter of the blaze contained, officials were left hoping for rain — just not too much, as communities near fire burn scars are now fearing flash floods and mudslides.

“Really,” Mr. Cox said, “we need some help from Mother Nature.”

Madaleine Rubin contributed reporting.

item.title: Hunter Biden Says His Father’s Cancer Is Worsening
Max Miller, Republican Accused of Abuse, Won’t Drop Out, Spokeswoman Says
item.description:
Representative Max Miller, the Republican from Ohio accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, has defied calls from his own party to drop out and plans to stay in the race to keep his seat in Congress, according to his spokeswoman.

Mr. Miller would have had to withdraw by Saturday evening, at the latest, to allow local party chairs enough time to name a replacement on the ballot by Monday at 4 p.m., according to Ohio state law.

His decision, confirmed by Abigail Angelos, a campaign spokeswoman, sets up a competitive general-election campaign. Mr. Miller’s district was considered solidly Republican before his divorce from the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio and the public allegations of physical abuse that followed.

Mr. Miller has denied the accusations, which include holding a gun to his ex-wife’s head, throwing scalding water at her and fracturing the collarbone of their daughter.

Over the past week, pressure mounted from within his party for him to step aside. President Trump called Mr. Miller, a former aide to the president, to encourage him to look carefully at his odds. Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican also up for re-election, described him as unfit for office and urged him to resign from Congress. White House staff members and Republican officials in Ohio have privately conveyed concerns that his personal problems could cost the party a seat as it tries to keep control of the House.

But Mr. Miller has been resolute all week that he planned to do what Mr. Trump had done when faced with his own personal scandals: stay in and fight. He has defended himself in a media tour that left some in his own party worried about his mental state and alarmed at the prospect of his continued candidacy.

In November, he will face Brian Poindexter, a union-card-carrying ironworker who Democrats believe can defeat Mr. Miller with an appeal to the working-class voters in Ohio’s Seventh District.

The Ohio Republican Party and local party chairs stayed publicly quiet this week, for the most part, declining to answer questions about whether they supported Mr. Miller’s candidacy.

If Mr. Miller had withdrawn, they would have had to call a meeting by the end of Saturday to replace him, under state law.

Matt Miller, the chairman of the Ashland County Republican Party and the mayor of Ashland, who is not related to the congressman, said on Saturday that no such meeting had been scheduled.

item.title: Beth, the Beloved Vacuum of a 92-Year-Old Iowa Senator, Has Died
item.description:
Beth, a trusty tan Hoover vacuum cleaner with a burgundy cloth dust bag that for years tended to the floors of the Iowa farmhouse of Senator Chuck Grassley, earning admirers in both parties, has died. She was believed to be 49.

The cause was apparently an electrical problem, said Mr. Grassley, a Republican who often admiringly posted images of his cleaning companion on social media around Christmas, Thanksgiving, Easter and family reunions.

“U willl see Beth no more,” Mr. Grassley, 92 and the oldest senator, wrote on social media on Saturday, attaching an image that showed Beth’s electrical cord connector scarred by sparks. “See black that’s from electrical sparks. It’s not safe to use anymore. GOOD BYE BETH.”

It’s a sad day at Grassley household…. For my 34 years and 15 yrs before that at my mother in law’s home Beth has worked dependably….

He declared it a “sad day at Grassley household” and recalled that Beth had worked “dependably” for 34 years at his home, and for 15 years before that at his mother-in-law’s house. He wrote of Beth, “U hv been a real workhorse,” adding, “I will miss u.”

Year after year, around the holidays and during other occasions when cleaning was in order, Mr. Grassley would fire up Beth. The vacuum, he said, allowed him to make a contribution to the festivities as others in the family prepared food.

At roughly 49, Beth had been at work since before Mr. Grassley, a corn and soybean farmer, reached the Senate in 1981. The vacuum was also older than several U.S. senators.

But Beth drew public notice only in recent years, when Mr. Grassley, who has an irreverent style on social media, began to post about his vacuum. (In 2020, Mr. Grassley announced the death of a pigeon by writing on social media, “If u lost ur pet pidgin /it’s dead in front yard my Iowa farm JUST DISCOVERED.”)

Two days before Thanksgiving in 2018, Mr. Grassley wrote on social media: “Mrs G and daughter Wendy hv started big job of preparing meal for30 at farm Thxgiving. So my housework contribution begins. This is my machine (Beth).”

He made a habit of such posts.

“Faithful Beth has about 3 hours of cleaning to get ready for 25/30 grassley family,” he wrote on Christmas in 2022.

For Thanksgiving in 2023, he shared a video of Beth roaring across a rug as he pushed the vacuum and shuffled behind it.

The same year, Mr. Grassley posted an image of him and Senator Shelley Moore Capito, Republican of West Virginia, holding a cutout image of Beth. “Turns out Senator Capito is a big fan of Beth,” he wrote.

Beth had, by any measure, an extraordinarily long life for an upright vacuum cleaner. A typical vacuum might last for eight years, according to Consumer Reports, though life spans vary by brand.

Hoover says that its upright vacuums last eight years on average, and that its cordless vacuums are good for about five years on average.

Techtronic Industries, which owns Hoover, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Beth’s demise.

But within hours of Mr. Grassley’s announcement, others in politics had begun to take note, and to offer condolences.

“Sorry for your loss, Senator,” Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative in Iowa running for the state’s other Senate seat, wrote Saturday evening on social media. “Sounds like Beth had a heck of a run.”

item.title: Moderate Democrat in Hawaii Defeats Progressive House Challenger
item.description:
Representative Ed Case, a moderate Democrat from Hawaii, warded off a progressive challenger in his primary race on Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

His victory defies a larger trend of left-wing challengers ousting pro-Israel incumbents this year. Mr. Case, 73, is also among the few older, centrist Democrats who have hung onto their seats after serious primary challenges.

The strongest of Mr. Case’s primary opponents was Jarrett Keohokalole, a state senator 30 years his junior. Mr. Keohokalole argued that Mr. Case was out of touch with the struggles of ordinary people in Hawaii as the cost of living has skyrocketed, and that he was not speaking out enough against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

With an estimated 84 percent of the expected vote reported, Mr. Case led Mr. Keohokalole 60.2 percent to 35.9 percent.

Mr. Case is among the most fiscally conservative Democrats in the House and has repeatedly broken ranks with his party, angering some on the left. He has represented Hawaii’s First District, anchored in Honolulu, since 2019.

Mr. Keohokalole criticized Mr. Case’s vote last year for legislation pushed by President Trump that would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote. (Mr. Case told Hawaii News Now that he no longer supported the measure after Republicans stripped an option for voters to attest to their citizenship in writing if they lack documentation.) Mr. Keohokalole said that unlike Mr. Case, he would not vote to send military aid to Israel for the war on Gaza.

But generational change was perhaps the central theme of the campaign. One of Mr. Keohokalole’s ads featured a staticky video of Mr. Case saying during his 2006 bid for the U.S. Senate: “It is time for the next generation of leadership. We just need the courage to choose it.” (That year, Mr. Case, then 53, was challenging Senator Daniel Akaka, then 82, in the Democratic primary.)

The ad then cut to Mr. Keohokalole, 43, who said: “It’s 20 years later, and things aren’t going well. Families are leaving, and Washington still isn’t listening. Hawaii deserves a representative that’s living what you’re living.”

In response, Mr. Case argued that the state needed his seniority and expertise to reap the most in federal benefits. He emphasized his spot on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which sets the budget.

“Without good representation in Congress, we’d just get lost,” Mr. Case said in one television ad. “Every day, I use my seniority and service on Appropriations to fight for our Hawaii, including billions of dollars in federal assistance every year. In uncertain times, strong, steady, experienced leadership matters.”

A former majority leader of the state’s House of Representatives, Mr. Case represented Hawaii’s Second Congressional District from 2002 to 2007 after winning a special election to fill the seat held by Representative Patsy Mink, who died days after Mr. Case lost the 2002 Democratic primary for governor. Mr. Case returned to Washington in 2019 to represent the First Congressional District and has held the seat since. His family came to Hawaii from Kansas in 1896, according to his campaign website.

Mr. Case’s victory in the solidly blue district makes it highly likely that he will win re-election in November.
